I've been active in the Swedish tournament scene as a judge for the
last 3 years and I must tell that during these years I have never ever
had to punish a player for premeditated (spelling?) cheating. I use
sleeves and I use decklists at our bigger events. But still, this fear
of cheating is getting a bit absurd. Can someone enlighten me about
events when they have been forced to punish people for cheating?

> About the disqualification thing, i'll let the final word here to our head
> judge for the event -
> we adopted the same line with the italian qualifiers and championship past
> years, and all

Sure thing. Keep the decklists. But be aware that a good judge is a
judge who can read a situation and act from it with objective fairness
in his judgement. So I plead to you, use the decklist DQ's with sense.
Don't repeat the mistakes of the past. For instance, player A gets into
the final of the EC and the checking of his deck shows that he is
missing a fame. If I were to follow the information that's on the EC
2006 website I as a judge would have to DQ him/her.
Please don't do this, use decklists, but also use common sense when
faced with incorrect decklists.

Thats all for now!

Alex Ek
VEKN Prince of Gothenburg, Sweden

The flaw has been pointed out.

The fact that disqualification is automatic (according to the EC2006
web site: "Any irregularities in deck and/or decklist will result in
the player being disqualified") is both unfair and excessive, and
against the Judges' Guide, where such infractions have either a
"warning" penalty or a "game loss" penalty.

Perhaps some of you do not know that issuing a disqualification penalty
to a player with a wrong deck/decklist was addressed for the first time
in a Continental Qualifier/Championship (AFAIK) in the Barcelona EC
(2003). However, that was not a disqualification by default, but a
speciffic penalty issued instead of a game loss happening prior to the
start of the final round, because the Archon cannot handle a game loss
in such circumstances, so disqualifying the infractor was the only way
for the Archon to move the next highest ranked player to the final
round.

EXCERPT FROM THE EC 2003 JUDGING CRITERIA
Illegal decks: Decks will be inspected at random during the three
preliminary rounds of both the Spanish Qualifier and the European
Championship. And all of the finalists' decks will be inspected before
the start of the final. If a player's deck is proven illegal after the
third round has finished (before the start of the final), and the
appropriate penalty for the infraction in the V:EKN Judges Guidelines
is a game loss, judges will disqualify that player instead. The next
highest ranked player in the tournament will then take his or her place
in the final round. If a judge determines that a deck has been
improperly reassembled (if you accidentally scoop up a Haven Uncovered
on one of your minions and place it in your library resulting in a
91-card library between rounds, for instance), that deck will not be
considered illegal, and that player should make any changes necessary
to make the contents of the deck match what is recorded on the
decklist.

--

At major events, judges very often have to make decisions which are seen
as controversial by some subset of the people there - such as those
people detrimentally affected by them, the people who travelled with
them, people from the same playgroup/town/country as them, people who
have a preferred play-style (such as those who view any sort of VP split
deal-making as bad, and whose tolerance for such deals is significantly
below what the judge regards as being appropriate, based on his or her
understanding of the rules on the subject).

Judges having to make controversial decisions is not a new problem. And
rigid application of rules when there are obviously screwed up
circumstances (a table was knocked over, causing decks to be scattered,
for example) will be similarly controversial.

If people think that rigid application of over-the-top rules without
regard to, you know, sanity will prevent controversial decisions being
made, they're wrong.
